fable-5.1.text:
I'd first gently push back on the framing a little, because I don't think it's strictly either-or. But if you ask me where I'd put my own effort right now, I'd pick memory, and the reason is pretty simple: memory is a prerequisite, and collaboration is something you can layer on top once the prerequisite is there.

Think about what a single agent actually does today. You give it a long task, it works for a while, and after some number of steps it starts to lose track of what it already tried, what the user told it earlier, what constraints it discovered along the way. The context window is a very crude form of memory. It's expensive, it's finite, and the model doesn't really know what to keep and what to throw away. So a lot of the failure cases people attribute to "reasoning" are actually failures of remembering. The agent didn't get the step wrong, it forgot the premise.

Now, if that's the situation for one agent, what happens when you put five of them together? You don't get five times the capability. You get five agents that each have a partial, slightly inconsistent picture of the task, and now they also have to spend a lot of tokens talking to each other to re-synchronize. A lot of the multi-agent results I've seen are essentially compensating for weak memory with communication. You split the problem because no single agent can hold the whole thing in its head, and then you pay a coordination cost to stitch it back. If each agent could just remember well, a good fraction of that architecture becomes unnecessary.

There's also a practical research argument. Memory is a well-defined problem with clear evaluation. Does the agent retain this fact after ten thousand steps? Does it retrieve the right thing at the right time? Does it update when the world changes? You can measure that. Collaboration between agents is much harder to study cleanly, because the behavior depends on the memory, the communication protocol, the task decomposition, and which model you used, all at once. When something goes wrong, you often can't tell which piece broke. I tend to prefer working on the layer below where I can actually isolate variables.

And from an architecture perspective, I find memory more interesting because I think it's where the next real change in the model itself might come from. Coming from the vision side, a lot of my past work was about finding simple designs that scale well. Right now, the way we handle long-horizon information in these models is not simple and does not scale well. It's a bunch of retrieval heuristics and summarization tricks bolted onto a fixed-context transformer. Whatever eventually replaces that, whether it's a better recurrent state, learned compression, or something we haven't thought of, that's going to matter for every agent, collaborative or not.

So my view is, get one agent to remember like a competent person remembers across a long project. Once you have that, collaboration becomes a much easier and much more honest problem to study, because you'll actually know that the gains come from working together and not from patching over forgetfulness.

opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say collaboration doesn't matter. I just think the order matters, and right now memory is the bottleneck that limits everything else.

Look at how agents work today. You give one a task, it does something reasonable for twenty minutes or an hour, and then the context fills up, or the session ends, and almost everything it learned is gone. The next time you ask it something similar, it starts from scratch. It doesn't remember that this codebase has a weird build system, or that you prefer a certain style, or that it already tried approach A and it failed. A human employee who forgot everything at the end of each day wouldn't be very useful, no matter how smart they were in the moment.

So when people say "let's have ten agents collaborate," my question is: collaborate on top of what? If each agent can't accumulate experience, you're basically coordinating ten very capable amnesiacs. You can get some gains from parallelism, splitting up a task, having one agent check another's work. But a lot of what makes human teams productive comes from shared, persistent context: people remember what was decided last week, who knows what, what went wrong before. Without good memory, multi-agent systems end up spending a huge fraction of their effort re-communicating context to each other, and things get lost in every handoff.

There's also a more research-flavored reason. I think memory is close to the question of continual learning, which is one of the big unsolved problems. Right now our models learn in one giant pretraining phase, and after that they're essentially frozen. Everything at deployment time is in-context. The ability to actually accumulate knowledge from experience, deciding what to keep, compressing it, retrieving the right thing at the right time, maybe eventually writing some of it back into the weights, seems much more fundamental than the orchestration layer of how agents talk to each other. Collaboration protocols feel more like an engineering problem we can solve reasonably well once the individual agents are more capable.

And if you get memory right, a lot of collaboration might come almost for free. A single agent that remembers well across long horizons can already do much of what we currently try to get from multiple agents. And when you do want multiple agents, a shared memory is probably the most natural way for them to coordinate anyway.

So my view is that collaboration is important, but it sits on top of memory. If we want agents working on tasks that take days or weeks, like real research projects or maintaining a large software system, persistent memory is the piece that's missing, and that's where I'd put the effort first.

fable-5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what's actually the bottleneck right now. When we look at where agents fail today, it's usually not because they lack a teammate — it's because they can't remember what happened an hour ago, or what they learned on the last task, or what the user told them last week. The fundamental unit is still a single agent, and that single agent is, frankly, amnesiac. It has a context window, and everything outside that window is essentially gone unless you bolt on some retrieval system, which tends to be shallow and brittle.

So if I build a collaborative system out of agents like that, I'm essentially assembling a team where every member has severe memory problems. Collaboration doesn't fix that — it compounds it. Now you have communication overhead, you have agents repeating work because nobody remembers it was already done, and errors propagate between agents instead of getting caught. Multi-agent systems are a multiplier on the capabilities of the individual agent, and if the individual is weak, you're multiplying a small number.

Whereas memory is what unlocks the things people actually want from agents: long-horizon tasks that span days or weeks, learning from experience so the agent doesn't make the same mistake twice, personalization so it actually knows you and your codebase and your preferences. And interestingly, a lot of what people use multi-agent setups for today — splitting a big task across agents — is really a workaround for limited context and memory. If a single agent could genuinely accumulate and organize knowledge over a long horizon, you wouldn't need the committee for many of those cases.

So it's not that collaboration is unimportant — I think it will matter eventually. It's a question of ordering. Memory is the foundational capability; collaboration is a layer you build on top once the foundation is solid. Right now I'd rather have one agent with a real memory than ten agents with none.

opus-5.text:
I'd push back slightly on the framing of "more important," but I do think there's a real asymmetry, so let me try to say why.

My honest read is that a lot of multi-agent work is a workaround for single-agent limitations rather than a capability in its own right. If you look at why people shard a task across five agents, very often it's because one agent can't hold the whole problem in its head — the context runs out, or it loses track of what it already tried. So you spin up subagents, each with a fresh window, and a coordinator that stitches summaries back together. That's a memory architecture wearing a collaboration costume. And it's a lossy one, because the interface between agents is a few hundred tokens of natural language summary, which is a terrible channel compared to just... remembering.

The other thing is that collaboration frameworks tend to be the kind of hand-designed scaffolding that gets washed out as the base models improve. I've watched this happen repeatedly in vision — people build elaborate pipelines around a weak component, the component gets stronger, and the pipeline evaporates. Memory doesn't feel like that to me. It's not scaffolding around a missing capability; it *is* the missing capability. An agent that works on my codebase today and starts from zero tomorrow is never going to get good at my codebase, no matter how good its single-episode reasoning gets. Humans are useful collaborators largely because they accumulate — the second month is better than the first.

Where I'd concede ground: parallelism is genuinely valuable, and there are tasks where you want adversarial structure, like having one model critique another. Those aren't memory in disguise.

But if I had a student deciding what to work on, I'd say the memory problem is more likely to still be the bottleneck in three years. Multi-agent orchestration mostly isn't a research problem, it's an engineering one, and it's downstream of solving memory anyway.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say collaboration doesn't matter, but I think memory is the more fundamental problem, and a lot of what people want from collaboration depends on it.

Right now, most agents are stateless in the ways that count. You start a session, give it context, and it does something useful. Then the session ends and it's gone, or you get a thin summary that loses most of what mattered. A human colleague gets better at working with you over time. They remember your preferences, what you tried last month, what failed, and why you made a certain decision. Without that, an agent is always a new hire on their first day, however smart it is.

Memory is also what lets an agent learn from experience without retraining the model. If an agent can reliably store what it learned from a task and retrieve it at the right moment, it improves just by being used. That gets us closer to the long-horizon, continual-learning behavior we want. It's also hard. It isn't only about storing more tokens or a longer context window. It's about deciding what to keep, how to compress it, when to forget, and how to retrieve it when it's relevant.

On collaboration, I think a lot of multi-agent setups today are partly a workaround for limited context and limited capability. You split the task across agents because one agent can't hold everything in its head. If one agent had good memory and could work over a long horizon, you'd need less of that scaffolding. And collaboration itself needs memory. Agents can't build shared understanding, divide work, or hold each other accountable if each one forgets what happened an hour ago.

So I see memory as the more basic capability, and collaboration builds on top of it. If I had to pick where to put research effort first, I'd pick memory.

haiku-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing, because I don't think it's really either-or. But if I have to pick, memory comes first. Collaboration sits on top of individual competence and continuity. Two agents that forget everything between sessions can pass messages back and forth, but they can't build shared understanding, remember what the other one tried last week, or learn from yesterday's mistakes.

Most of the failures I see in agents right now aren't coordination failures. An agent rediscovers the same codebase conventions every time, forgets a constraint the user gave it three steps earlier, or repeats an approach it already knows doesn't work. Those are memory failures. Adding more agents to a system that can't hold onto what it knows just multiplies the forgetting.

I also think the memory problem is harder than people assume. It isn't just a bigger context window or a vector database full of transcripts. The hard part is deciding what to keep, how to compress it, when to revise something you believed, and when to let it go. Human memory is useful because it's selective and lossy in the right ways, and I don't think we have good answers yet for agents.

So my bet is that once single agents can accumulate and revise experience reliably, collaboration becomes much more tractable, because there's something stable to coordinate around.

astra-6.text:
I think memory is a more fundamental bottleneck. If you want an agent that works with you over a long period of time, it needs to remember what you’re trying to accomplish, what you’ve already tried, and what worked or didn’t work. Otherwise, you spend every interaction reconstructing the context, and the agent can keep making the same mistakes.

Having multiple agents collaborate could be useful, especially when a task benefits from different perspectives. But if none of them retains what it learns, adding more agents doesn’t really solve that continuity problem. You also introduce the problem of coordinating them.

And by memory, I don’t just mean storing every conversation. The interesting question is what to keep, how to update it, and when to bring it back into the agent’s reasoning. I’d prioritize that because it seems essential to making an agent useful beyond a single task. It could also make collaboration more effective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think memory is more fundamental because it determines whether an agent can accumulate experience. You want an agent to remember what you’ve worked on together, what your preferences are, and which approaches succeeded or failed. Otherwise, you spend a lot of time explaining the same things again, and the agent keeps making the same mistakes.

Collaboration can help you divide a task or get different perspectives. But if every agent has that same limitation, adding more agents also adds communication and coordination overhead. Someone still needs to keep track of what has been tried and what the overall goal is.

So I would prioritize making one agent useful over a long period of time. And memory is more than storing the entire conversation. The difficult part is deciding what to retain, when to retrieve it, and how to update it when something changes. If we solve that well, I think it will also make collaboration between agents much more effective.
